title: Triathlon equipment: overview
description: Triathlon equipment essentials: wetsuit, bike. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. The right gear does three things: keeps you safe, lets you perform, and lasts. Beginners should spend on safety and fit first — the best equipment is the kind you forget you are wearing because it fits perfectly and does its job.

title: Gear 1: wetsuit
description: In Triathlon, the wetsuit matters more than beginners think. Fit is everything — wrong size ruins performance and risks injury. Try before buying, break in gradually, and maintain it: clean it, dry it, store it properly. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Quality gear lasts years when cared for; neglected gear fails at the worst moment.

title: Footwear
d: Triathlon footwear must suit the surface.
definition: Triathlon footwear must suit the surface.
description: Footwear for Triathlon: matched to the surface, fitted to the foot, replaced on schedule. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. The wrong shoes cause the most common overuse injuries in sport. Break new pairs in gradually, keep them dry between sessions, and retire them when the support dies — usually long before they look worn.

title: Protective gear
d: Protection in Triathlon is mandatory where the laws require it.
definition: Protection in Triathlon is mandatory where the laws require it.
description: Protective gear in Triathlon: helmets, guards, and padding exist because the injury patterns are known. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Wear every required piece, every session — the one rep you skip is the one that finds you. Replace protective gear after any serious impact; its job was to die so you did not.

title: Apparel
d: Triathlon kit: built for movement, weather, and team identity.
definition: Triathlon kit: built for movement, weather, and team identity.
description: Apparel for Triathlon: moisture-wicking, unrestricted, and weather-appropriate. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Team kits carry identity — wear them with pride and keep them clean. In heat, light colors and ventilation; in cold, layers you can shed. Never let clothing restrict the movements the sport demands.

title: Training aids
d: Train Triathlon smarter with cones, targets, and video.
definition: Train Triathlon smarter with cones, targets, and video.
description: Training aids for Triathlon: cones, targets, rebounders, and video turn good sessions into great ones. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. The best aid is often the simplest — a wall, a target, a stopwatch. Buy aids that fix your specific weakness, not the gadget of the month.

title: Maintenance
d: Maintain Triathlon gear: clean, dry, inspect, store.
definition: Maintain Triathlon gear: clean, dry, inspect, store.
description: Maintenance for Triathlon equipment: clean after use, dry fully before storage, inspect before every session, store out of sun and damp. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. A five-minute routine doubles gear life. Keep a small repair kit — tape, laces, patches — because failures happen at venues, not at home.

title: Fitting guide
d: Fit Triathlon gear properly: the performance multiplier.
definition: Fit Triathlon gear properly: the performance multiplier.
description: Fitting Triathlon gear: the difference between good and great equipment is usually fit. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Get fitted by someone who knows the sport, re-check fit as young athletes grow, and never borrow safety gear. If it moves, pinches, or distracts, it does not fit.

title: Safety standards
d: Triathlon gear must meet certification standards.
definition: Triathlon gear must meet certification standards.
description: Safety standards for Triathlon: look for the certification marks — they mean the gear passed real tests. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Counterfeit safety gear kills; buy from reputable sources. Standards update over time; replace gear that predates current certifications.

title: Youth gear
d: Young Triathlon athletes need sized-down, not dumbed-down, gear.
definition: Young Triathlon athletes need sized-down, not dumbed-down, gear.
description: Youth Triathlon gear: sized for growing bodies, never adult hand-me-downs that do not fit. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Kids outgrow gear fast — buy adjustable where possible and check fit monthly. Never compromise on helmets or protection to save money; skimp on the bag, not the brain bucket.

title: Budget guide
d: Equip for Triathlon at any budget: spend on safety first.
definition: Equip for Triathlon at any budget: spend on safety first.
description: Budgeting Triathlon gear: spend first on protection and fit, then on the implement, last on accessories. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Good used gear beats bad new gear for non-safety items. Plan the yearly replacement cycle so costs never surprise you mid-season.

title: Innovations
d: Triathlon equipment keeps evolving: materials, data, and design.
definition: Triathlon equipment keeps evolving: materials, data, and design.
description: Innovation in Triathlon gear: lighter materials, smarter design, and embedded data. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Adopt innovations that solve your problem; ignore the rest until proven. The fundamentals — fit, safety, durability — outlast every trend.

title: Rules on equipment
d: The laws of Triathlon regulate equipment specifications.
definition: The laws of Triathlon regulate equipment specifications.
description: Equipment rules in Triathlon: the laws specify what is legal — dimensions, materials, and sometimes brands. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Check legality before competition; illegal gear means disqualification. When in doubt, ask an official before the event, not during it.

title: Equipment checklist
description: The Triathlon pre-session checklist: inspect every item, confirm fit, pack spares. Wetsuits add buoyancy; bikes are tri-specific. Five minutes of checking prevents the failures that ruin sessions — the forgotten mouthguard, the flat ball, the dead battery. Make the checklist a habit and the habit will save a season.
